explanation:
The reference reproduces all three demonstrations exactly, and the inspect run also confirms the one subtle part of it: without the "blocked path" check, train pair 1 fails at two cells. So I will keep the reference's logic, and explain it.

## What the grids are made of

Every input has two kinds of things on a black (0) background:

- grey 2x2 **blocks** (colour 5), which never move;
- single coloured **pixels** (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9), scattered around.

The fact sheet shows the output has exactly the same colour counts as the input and the grey blocks keep their bounding boxes. Only the single pixels change position: each "0→c" is paired with a "c→0". So the rule is purely a *movement* of pixels.

## Where a pixel goes

Compare a few moves in train pair 3, the cleanest case:

- 8 at (2,5) → (2,4): slides left until it touches the block at rows 1–2, cols 2–3.
- 6 at (4,14) → (5,14): slides down until it touches the block at rows 6–7, cols 13–14.
- 9 at (8,8) → (7,8): slides up to the block at rows 5–6, cols 6–7.
- 1 at (8,3) → (9,3): slides down to the block at rows 10–11.
- 6 at (12,9) → (12,10): slides right to the block at rows 10–11, cols 11–12.

So each pixel is **attracted to the nearest grey block** and ends up on the one-cell ring surrounding that block, as close as possible to where it started. Distance to a block is measured as Chebyshev distance to its bounding box (king moves), with Manhattan distance as a tiebreak. The pixel lands on the ring cell nearest to it; when it is on a row/column/diagonal of the block it stops right in line (that is the "slide" look); otherwise it takes the nearest corner-ish ring cell.

Train pair 2 shows that several pixels can share a block: 3 at (7,0), 8 at (5,2), 4 at (4,4) all crowd around the block at rows 1–2, cols 1–2, landing at (3,0), (3,2), (3,3) — each the closest free ring cell to its own start. Pixels are processed nearest-first, and a ring cell already taken is skipped, so the 2x2 block collects a little cluster of satellites.

## The one subtlety: a pixel in the way

Train pair 1 has 9 at (5,11) and 2 at (6,11), both directly under the block at rows 2–3, cols 10–11. The 9 slides up to (4,11). The 2 does *not* queue up under the same block — in the output it is at (9,11), touching the *lower* block at rows 10–11. The 9 was standing between the 2 and the upper block, so that block is treated as unreachable and the 2 takes its next-nearest block. My inspect confirmed that the plain "nearest block" rule mismatches the output exactly at this pixel (and at the cell it would have wrongly displaced), while the version with the obstruction test matches all three pairs. The obstruction test walks a king-move path from the pixel toward the point of the block's ring it would land on; if another *original* pixel lies on that path, the block is excluded.

## Applying it to the test input

Five grey blocks, nine pixels. Running the rule:

- 4 at (0,8): the block at rows 2–3, cols 12–13 is nearest, but the 9 at (1,11) sits exactly on its approach path, so it is excluded; the 4 goes to the top-left block and lands at (0,4), its corner cell.
- 9 at (1,11) already touches that right block's corner, so it stays.
- 8 at (7,13) slides up to (4,13); 7 at (5,1) goes to (5,2), the corner of the block at rows 6–7, cols 3–4; 2 at (7,8) slides left to (7,5).
- 8 at (9,8) slides down to (10,8); 9 at (9,11) goes to (10,10), the corner above the block at rows 11–12, cols 8–9.
- 3 at (13,4) slides left to (13,2); 6 at (13,13) slides left to (13,10).

The construction stages emitted are: clear all pixels, then place them one at a time (nearest-first) on their block's ring.
code:
def transform(grid):
    g = np.array(grid)
    bg = background(g)
    H, W = g.shape
    objs = objects(g, bg)
    blocks = [o["box"] for o in objs if o["size"] > 1]
    pix = [(o["cells"][0], o["colour"]) for o in objs if o["size"] == 1]
    pixset = {p for p, _ in pix}

    def boxdist(p, b):
        y, x = p
        y0, x0, y1, x1 = b
        dy = max(y0 - y, 0, y - y1)
        dx = max(x0 - x, 0, x - x1)
        return max(dy, dx), dy + dx

    def blocked(p, b):
        # walk (king moves) from the pixel to the ring cell it would hit;
        # another original pixel on the way makes this block unreachable
        y, x = p
        y0, x0, y1, x1 = b
        ty = min(max(y, y0 - 1), y1 + 1)
        tx = min(max(x, x0 - 1), x1 + 1)
        while (y, x) != (ty, tx):
            y += (ty > y) - (ty < y)
            x += (tx > x) - (tx < x)
            if (y, x) in pixset:
                return True
        return False

    plan = []
    for p, c in pix:
        cands = [(boxdist(p, b), i) for i, b in enumerate(blocks) if not blocked(p, b)]
        if not cands:
            cands = [(boxdist(p, b), i) for i, b in enumerate(blocks)]
        d, i = min(cands)
        plan.append((d, p, c, i))
    plan.sort()  # nearest pixels claim ring cells first

    out = g.copy()
    for _, p, c, _ in plan:
        out[p] = bg
    emit(out, "Lift every single coloured pixel off the canvas; only the grey 2x2 blocks stay in place.")

    occ = set()
    for d, p, c, i in plan:
        y0, x0, y1, x1 = blocks[i]
        ring = [(yy, xx) for yy in range(y0 - 1, y1 + 2) for xx in range(x0 - 1, x1 + 2)
                if 0 <= yy < H and 0 <= xx < W and not (y0 <= yy <= y1 and x0 <= xx <= x1)]

        def key(r):
            dy = r[0] - p[0]
            dx = r[1] - p[1]
            straight = dy == 0 or dx == 0 or abs(dy) == abs(dx)
            return (max(abs(dy), abs(dx)), not straight, abs(dy) + abs(dx), r)

        free = [r for r in ring if r not in occ]
        t = min(free, key=key)
        occ.add(t)
        out[t] = c
        emit(out, f"Pixel {c} at {p}: nearest reachable grey block is rows {y0}-{y1}, cols {x0}-{x1}; "
                  f"it moves to the closest free cell touching that block, {t}.")

    emit(out, "Every pixel now sits against its nearest grey block.")
    return out
